accepted.s: The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) of the European Union was implemented from which date?
accepted.x: The EU GDPR, adopted in April 2016, was implemented from 25 May 2018.
accepted.tq: Use the precise implementation date rather than the adoption date.
accepted.sec: Global frameworks - EU GDPR, right to erasure, right to be forgotten

accepted.s: Which of the following best describes the Right to Be Forgotten (RTBF)?
o: Removal, masking or de-indexing of outdated, irrelevant or harmful personal information
A right available only to government employees
Permanent deletion of every judicial record concerning a person
A right to prevent all forms of online identification
accepted.x: RTBF concerns the removal, masking or de-indexing of outdated, irrelevant or harmful personal information. It does not require the deletion of every judicial record.
accepted.tq: Identify the exact scope of the right instead of choosing an extreme formulation.
accepted.sec: Global frameworks - EU GDPR, right to erasure, right to be forgotten

accepted.s: The Right to Be Forgotten originated in the European case of:
o: Laksh Vir Singh Yadav v Union of India
Kharak Singh v State of Uttar Pradesh
accepted.x: The RTBF originated in Google Spain v AEPD (2014).
accepted.tq: Match the right with the case in which it originated.
accepted.sec: Global frameworks - EU GDPR, right to erasure, right to be forgotten

accepted.s: Under which provision of the GDPR was the Right to Be Forgotten formalised as the Right to Erasure?
accepted.x: The GDPR formalised the Right to Be Forgotten as the Right to Erasure under Article 17.
accepted.tq: Discriminate between closely related article and section numbers.
accepted.sec: Global frameworks - EU GDPR, right to erasure, right to be forgotten

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Right to Be Forgotten in India:
1. It forms part of the right to privacy under Article 21.
2. It is an absolute right applicable without any limitation.
3. It does not erase judicial records but may limit name-based searches.
4. Section 12 of the DPDP Act provides a Right to Erasure.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct. Statement 2 is false because the right is not absolute; it does not erase judicial records and may operate by limiting name-based searches.
accepted.tq: Find the statement that improperly converts a qualified right into an absolute one.
accepted.sec: Global frameworks - EU GDPR, right to erasure, right to be forgotten

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the Right to Be Forgotten from a general deletion of judicial records?
o: It applies only to biometric data collected by UIDAI.
It automatically cancels the judgment of a court.
It prohibits every search involving the person’s name.
It limits name-based searches without necessarily erasing judicial records.
accepted.x: The Indian understanding of RTBF does not erase judicial records; it can limit name-based searches in appropriate circumstances.
accepted.tq: Separate de-indexing or search limitation from destruction of the underlying record.
accepted.sec: Global frameworks - EU GDPR, right to erasure, right to be forgotten

accepted.s: Which case is associated with a framework for de-indexing name searches of acquitted persons by the Delhi High Court?
o: Laksh Vir Singh Yadav v Union of India
Gobind v State of Madhya Pradesh
accepted.x: The Delhi High Court case Laksh Vir Singh Yadav v. Union of India set a framework for de-indexing name searches of acquitted persons.
accepted.tq: Use the case-specific association rather than the broader constitutional source of privacy.
accepted.sec: Global frameworks - EU GDPR, right to erasure, right to be forgotten

accepted.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Concept/Authority)
 a. DPDP Act, 2023
 b. GDPR
 c. Indian data subject terminology
 d. EU data subject terminology

List-II (Term)
 i. Data Controller
 ii. Data Fiduciary
 iii. Data Subject
 iv. Data Principal

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
accepted.x: The DPDP Act uses Data Fiduciary and Data Principal, while the GDPR uses Data Controller and Data Subject.
accepted.tq: Start from the sure pair and eliminate codes with reversed terminology.
accepted.sec: Global frameworks - EU GDPR, right to erasure, right to be forgotten

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the DPDP Act, 2023 and the GDPR:
1. The DPDP Act covers only digital personal data, whereas the GDPR covers all personal data.
2. The DPDP Act provides for financial penalties only, while the GDPR may involve financial and criminal penalties in some states.
3. Data portability is an explicit right under the GDPR but is not a statutory right under the DPDP Act.
4. Both frameworks use the term ‘Data Fiduciary’ for the entity determining the purposes of processing.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because the GDPR uses ‘Data Controller’, whereas ‘Data Fiduciary’ is the DPDP Act terminology.
accepted.tq: Compare the frameworks row by row and detect the swapped legal term.
accepted.sec: Global frameworks - EU GDPR, right to erasure, right to be forgotten

accepted.s: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched regarding cross-border data treatment?
o: DPDP Act — blacklist approach, subject to restrictions
DPDP Act — whitelist or adequacy approach only
GDPR — cross-border transfers linked with adequacy
accepted.x: The DPDP Act is described as following a blacklist approach, allowing transfers unless restricted. The whitelist or adequacy approach is associated with the GDPR.
accepted.tq: Find the reversed comparison in the cross-border transfer row.
accepted.sec: Global frameworks - EU GDPR, right to erasure, right to be forgotten

accepted.s: Under the DPDP Act, 2023, the adjudicatory regulator is the:
o: Data Protection Authority of each State
accepted.x: The Data Protection Board of India is the adjudicatory regulator under the DPDP Act, 2023.
accepted.tq: Identify the exact statutory body instead of a similarly named authority.
accepted.sec: Global frameworks - EU GDPR, right to erasure, right to be forgotten

accepted.s: Which statement correctly compares the regulators under the DPDP Act and the GDPR?
o: The DPDP Act provides for the Data Protection Board of India, while the GDPR operates through a Data Protection Authority in each member state.
The DPDP Act provides for one DPA in every member state, while the GDPR provides for one national Board in India.
Both frameworks provide for the same single regulator at the international level.
Neither framework provides an adjudicatory or regulatory authority.
accepted.x: The DPDP Act provides for the Data Protection Board of India, whereas the GDPR framework has a Data Protection Authority in each member state.
accepted.tq: Keep the institutional comparison aligned with the jurisdiction of each framework.
accepted.sec: Global frameworks - EU GDPR, right to erasure, right to be forgotten

accepted.s: The maximum financial penalty specifically associated with the DPDP Act in the comparison of the two frameworks is:
accepted.x: The DPDP Act comparison specifies financial penalties of up to Rs 250 crore.
accepted.tq: Read the penalty figure precisely and reject altered magnitudes.
accepted.sec: Global frameworks - EU GDPR, right to erasure, right to be forgotten

accepted.s: Which constitutional provision was used in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) to declare privacy a Fundamental Right?
accepted.x: The nine-judge Bench declared the Right to Privacy a Fundamental Right under Article 21 and Part III of the Constitution. The judgment was also linked with Article 19 in the constitutional discussion.
accepted.tq: Identify the principal constitutional provision rather than a related procedural article.
accepted.sec: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017) - bench, right, basis, tests

accepted.s: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) was decided by:
o: A five-judge Bench by a majority of 4:1
accepted.x: The Puttaswamy privacy judgment was delivered by a unanimous nine-judge Bench on 24 August 2017.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the bench strength and voting pattern from the later Aadhaar judgment.
accepted.sec: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017) - bench, right, basis, tests

accepted.s: On which date was the nine-judge Puttaswamy privacy judgment delivered?
accepted.x: The unanimous nine-judge Puttaswamy judgment was delivered on 24 August 2017.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the Puttaswamy date from the Aadhaar judgment date.
accepted.sec: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017) - bench, right, basis, tests

accepted.s: The Puttaswamy judgment directed the government to:
accepted.x: The judgment directed the government to enact a data-protection law.
accepted.tq: Match the judgment with its institutional and legislative direction.
accepted.sec: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017) - bench, right, basis, tests

accepted.s: Which of the following cases were overruled by the Puttaswamy judgment to the extent that they denied privacy?
o: Aadhaar and Laksh Vir Singh Yadav
accepted.x: Puttaswamy overruled M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) to the extent that those decisions denied a constitutional right to privacy.
accepted.tq: Use the paired-case association and distinguish it from cases recognising privacy concerns.
accepted.sec: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017) - bench, right, basis, tests

accepted.s:
Arrange the following cases in chronological order:
A. Puttaswamy v Union of India
B. Gobind v State of Madhya Pradesh
C. Kharak Singh v State of Uttar Pradesh
D. M.P. Sharma v Satish Chandra
accepted.x: The correct sequence is M.P. Sharma (1954), Kharak Singh (1962), Gobind (1975), and Puttaswamy (2017).
accepted.tq: Fix the earliest and latest cases first, then place the two intervening cases by year.
accepted.sec: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017) - bench, right, basis, tests

accepted.s:
Match the following cases with the propositions associated with them:

List-I (Case)
 a. Kharak Singh v State of Uttar Pradesh
 b. Gobind v State of Madhya Pradesh
 c. Puttaswamy v Union of India

List-II (Proposition)
 i. Privacy recognised as part of personal liberty
 ii. Privacy recognised as a Fundamental Right and informational privacy affirmed
 iii. Early recognition of privacy concerns under Article 21

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
accepted.x: Kharak Singh is associated with early privacy concerns under Article 21; Gobind recognised privacy as part of personal liberty; Puttaswamy affirmed privacy as a Fundamental Right and informational privacy.
accepted.tq: Start with the distinctive Puttaswamy pair and then distinguish the two earlier recognitions.
accepted.sec: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017) - bench, right, basis, tests

accepted.s: The constitutional test for State intrusion into the right to privacy consists of:
accepted.x: The three-part test for State intrusion is legality, legitimate aim and proportionality.
accepted.tq: Recall the three-part constitutional test as a complete sequence.
accepted.sec: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017) - bench, right, basis, tests

accepted.s: A State measure interferes with informational privacy. To satisfy the test associated with Puttaswamy, which combination must be examined?
o: Whether it is supported by a private contract alone
Whether it has legality, a legitimate aim and proportionality
Whether it affects only citizens and not residents
Whether it has parliamentary privilege, secrecy and permanence
accepted.x: State intrusion into privacy is tested through legality, legitimate aim and proportionality.
accepted.tq: Apply the three-part test to a short constitutional scenario.
accepted.sec: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017) - bench, right, basis, tests

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements about the Aadhaar judgment of 2018:
1. It was decided by a five-judge Bench.
2. The decision was by a majority of 4:1.
3. Justice D.Y. Chandrachud dissented.
4. The judgment was delivered on 26 September 2018.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All four statements are correct: the Aadhaar judgment was delivered by a five-judge Bench on 26 September 2018 by 4:1, with Justice D.Y. Chandrachud dissenting.
accepted.tq: Combine bench strength, majority, dissent and date in one constitutional case cluster.
accepted.sec: Aadhaar judgment 2018 - provisions struck down and upheld

accepted.s: Which of the following was upheld in the Aadhaar judgment?
o: Section 57 permitting use by private entities without limitation
Mandatory Aadhaar linking with all bank accounts
Mandatory Aadhaar requirement for welfare benefits under Section 7
Mandatory linking of Aadhaar with mobile SIM cards
accepted.x: The Aadhaar Act was upheld, including mandatory Aadhaar for welfare benefits under Section 7. Mandatory linking with bank accounts and mobile SIMs was not upheld, and Section 57 relating to private entities was struck down.
accepted.tq: Distinguish upheld welfare use from the private and unrelated-linking provisions struck down or read down.
accepted.sec: Aadhaar judgment 2018 - provisions struck down and upheld

accepted.s: The Aadhaar judgment upheld Aadhaar-based linking for which of the following?
o: All mobile SIM connections as a general requirement
PAN and income-tax returns under Section 139AA of the Income-tax Act
accepted.x: The judgment upheld Aadhaar linking with PAN and income-tax returns under Section 139AA of the Income-tax Act.
accepted.tq: Identify the specific statutory linkage that was upheld among several broader claims.
accepted.sec: Aadhaar judgment 2018 - provisions struck down and upheld

accepted.s: Which one of the following was struck down or read down in the Aadhaar judgment?
o: The Aadhaar Act itself in its entirety
Section 57 concerning use by private entities
Section 139AA concerning PAN and income-tax returns
accepted.x: Section 57 of the Aadhaar Act, concerning use by private entities, was struck down. The Aadhaar Act was upheld, as were Section 7 welfare authentication and Section 139AA linkage.
accepted.tq: Find the provision belonging to the struck-down column rather than the upheld column.
accepted.sec: Aadhaar judgment 2018 - provisions struck down and upheld

accepted.s: The Aadhaar judgment did NOT uphold mandatory Aadhaar requirements relating to:
o: The Aadhaar Act and income-tax returns
Welfare benefits under Section 7 and PAN linking
Bank accounts, mobile SIMs, and specified educational examinations or admissions
accepted.x: Mandatory linking with bank accounts and mobile SIMs, as well as requirements relating to CBSE, NEET, UGC and school admissions, was struck down or not upheld.
accepted.tq: Group the provisions in the rejected category and watch for the EXCEPT-style reversal.
accepted.sec: Aadhaar judgment 2018 - provisions struck down and upheld

accepted.s: Which of the following was among the criticisms of the Aadhaar framework at the time of the 2018 judgment?
o: Lack of any provision for welfare authentication
Biometric data risks and absence of a data-protection law
accepted.x: The criticisms included risks associated with biometric data, the absence of a data-protection law, and mandatory linking requirements.
accepted.tq: Select the criticism that matches the privacy and data-protection concerns.
accepted.sec: Aadhaar judgment 2018 - provisions struck down and upheld

accepted.s: Aadhaar is best described as:
o: A sixteen-digit number issued by the Reserve Bank of India
A ten-digit number issued by the Data Protection Board of India
An eight-digit number issued by the Election Commission
A twelve-digit number issued by UIDAI
accepted.x: Aadhaar is a 12-digit number issued by the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI).
accepted.tq: Test both the numerical format and the issuing authority together.
accepted.sec: Aadhaar judgment 2018 - provisions struck down and upheld
